newsitem.title: CHINA: HK court hears landmark constitutional challenge.
newsitem.headline: HK court hears landmark constitutional challenge.

text.p: A criminal trial has become the springboard for a landmark challenge to the legitimacy of Hong Kong's post-colonial legal system, stoking fears of a constitutional crisis less than a month into Chinese rule.
Three Hong Kong heavyweight lawyers took over the case voluntarily on Wednesday, as the judicial temperature heated up, for a face-off with the government's own top lawyer.

Gladys Li, a stalwart of Hong Kong's British-based system of common law and one-time chairman of the bar, and former pro-democracy legislator and lawyer Margaret Ng, linked up with human rights lawyer Paul Harris for the showdown against Solicitor General Daniel Fung.

Lawyers argued on Tuesday that three people charged with criminal conspiracy should be set free because pre-handover laws under which they were charged had ceased to be valid on July 1 when a new legislature appointed by China failed formally to adopt them, leaving a legal vacuum.
The argument amounts to a challenge to the legitimacy of the Provisional Legislature and the entire legal system.

London handed the 156-year-old British colony back to Beijing as a special Chinese region three weeks ago. The capitalist outpost of 6.4 million people is supposed to keep its separate system and way of life unchanged for 50 years and more.
The three star lawyers jumped into the fray after two barristers, or criminal lawyers, complained the government was witholding legal financial aid for them to continue the case.
As the appeal court hearing reopened for its second day on Wednesday, the influential English-language South China Morning Post criticised the government for refusing legal aid.
"This is a matter which goes far beyond the interests of three accused men," it said in an editorial.
"It involves the very basis of the law and thus affects every citizen in Hong Kong and the legal framework within which busines is done here."

Defence lawyers have argued the Provisional Legislature did not adopt Hong Kong's Common Law when China took over, leaving it with no laws other than 13 ordinances adopted by the interim assembly under an act passed in the early hours of July 1.
It was not clear whether the case would conclude on Wednesday or drag on longer.
On Tuesday Solicitor General Fung argued that the appeal court had no power to rule on the legality of the legislature.
"The courts must accept the Provisional Legislative Council and the laws made by it," Fung said.
He said the legislature was established by the new sovereign power, China, and could not be challenged locally. "This is a matter purely of Chinese national law," he argued.
Fung warned that Hong Kong could be plunged into a crisis if the landmark challenge to the interim legislature succeeded.

The case has arisen as Hong Kong Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa grapples with a host of other problems, including opposition to his rollback of civil rights, his plan to deport child illegal immigrants back to China and his freezing of labour rights laws.
